clue.text: Charm of Dutch navigator, about 51

indicators.note: about means the navigator's name goes round the Roman numeral that follows

parts.note: Abel Tasman was the Dutch navigator who reached Tasmania and New Zealand
LI is 51 in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: Someone admires a lucky charm once owned by a Dutch explorer, dated roughly to fifty-one.
explanation.walkthrough: Abel Tasman was the seventeenth-century Dutch explorer after whom Tasmania is named; 51 is a Roman numeral here.
explanation.definitionFit: A talisman is an object thought to bring luck or ward off harm, the same as a lucky charm.

clue.text: Reprimands objectional little person so very loud

parts.note: tick is British slang for a contemptible little person
taken as written
FF is fortissimo, the musical marking for very loud

explanation.surface: Someone tells off an obnoxious little person for being so noisy.
explanation.walkthrough: TICK is British slang for an annoying, worthless person. FF (fortissimo) is the score marking for very loud. 'objectional' is printed as it appears in the source.
explanation.definitionFit: To tick someone off is a British idiom for scolding or telling them off.

clue.text: Piece of music left by organ with no name on getting mangled

indicators.note: getting mangled says the remaining letters are twisted into a new order
with no means the letter for name is dropped from organ

explanation.surface: A musical piece is wrecked when the organ loses its name-stop and gets mangled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with no' drops the N, leaving ORGA, which 'getting mangled' rearranges; 'on' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Largo is a slow, broad movement or composition, a tempo marking used as the name of a piece.

clue.text: A man set out to be a composer

indicators.note: out signals the letters are set out of their order, rearranged

explanation.surface: A man ventures forth intending to become a composer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' rearranges the seven letters of A MAN SET.
explanation.definitionFit: Bedrich Smetana was a Czech composer, best known for Ma Vlast and The Bartered Bride.

clue.text: Notice vermouth in the passage

parts.note: an ad is a notice or advertisement
It is short for Italian vermouth, as in gin and It

explanation.surface: Someone spots a vermouth advert while walking down a corridor.
explanation.walkthrough: IT for Italian vermouth comes from the old British bar order 'gin and It'.
explanation.definitionFit: An adit is a horizontal passage leading into a mine.

clue.text: The high point is OAP getting drunk — gosh!

indicators.note: getting drunk suggests something reeling and tipsy, so its letters stagger into a new order

parts.note: gee is an exclamation of surprise like gosh

explanation.surface: A pensioner getting tipsy is the night's highlight, to everyone's surprise.
explanation.walkthrough: OAP is British shorthand for old-age pensioner; 'getting drunk' rearranges it to APO, then GEE follows.
explanation.definitionFit: An apogee is the farthest point of an orbit, hence figuratively a peak or climax.

clue.text: A diary agent set up for providing item of garden furniture

indicators.note: in a down clue set up means the whole run is read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: a log is a diary or record kept day by day
a rep is a sales agent or representative

explanation.surface: A secretary arranges diary and agent for a garden-furniture supplier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'set up' turns the whole of A + LOG + REP, giving PER + GOL + A.
explanation.definitionFit: A pergola is an arched framework over a garden path, a garden structure for climbing plants.

clue.text: Vegetable even to be eaten by grandma

indicators.note: eaten by means the other letters sit inside grandma's word, as if swallowed

parts.note: gran is a familiar word for grandma
e'en is the poetic contraction of even
taken as written

explanation.surface: Even grandma ends up eating her vegetables.
explanation.walkthrough: The old poetic contraction of 'even', as in hymns and Shakespeare, drops the middle V; 'to' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A green bean is the edible pod of a bean plant, eaten as a vegetable.

clue.text: Number in the back of taxi!

parts.note: the final two letters of the word taxi are X and I, which together read as a Roman numeral

explanation.surface: Someone points out a figure sitting in the rear seat of a cab.
explanation.walkthrough: The last two letters of TAXI, X and I, read as the Roman numeral for the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Eleven is a whole number, one more than ten.

clue.text: 'Live for now?!' complained one, joining them

parts.note: carped means complained or found fault
I is the Roman numeral one
'em is the informal short form of them

explanation.surface: Someone grumbled about a carefree motto but joined the others anyway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'EM is the clipped colloquial form of 'them'.
explanation.definitionFit: Carpe diem, Latin for seize the day, is the motto urging people to enjoy the present.

clue.text: Scotsman on a mission shorrtly finds monkeys

parts.note: Mac is a nickname for a Scotsman

indicators.note: shortly, as misprinted, signals that the word for mission is cut short at its end

parts.note: a quest is a mission or search

explanation.surface: A Scot on an expedition soon comes across monkeys.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shorrtly' (printed with a doubled R) trims the last letter T from QUEST. MAC is a traditional nickname for a Scot.
explanation.definitionFit: Macaques are a genus of Old World monkeys, including the rhesus and Barbary apes.

clue.text: Old official showing hesitation around temptress

indicators.note: around here means turned round, so the hesitation sound is read backwards

parts.note: er is the sound of hesitation
Eve tempted Adam with the apple in Genesis

explanation.surface: An old official shows hesitation when faced with a seductive woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'around' looks like a container signal, but putting the hesitation round the temptress gives no word; here 'around' means turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: A reeve was a medieval English local magistrate or manor officer.

clue.text: Catchword in article coming after hard work

indicators.note: coming after puts the article behind the word for hard work

parts.note: a slog is a spell of hard, tiring work
an is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A catchphrase appears in a newspaper piece written after much toil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'coming after' reverses the clue's order, so the article goes at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A slogan is a short memorable phrase or motto, much like a catchword.

clue.text: Somehow get no urges sadly, having caught cold

indicators.note: having caught means the cold letter is held inside the rearranged letters
sadly says the letters of no urges are in a sorry, disordered state

parts.note: C is the standard abbreviation for cold, as on taps

explanation.surface: Someone sadly loses all their desires after catching a cold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sadly' rearranges NO URGES; 'having caught' puts C inside, after the S.
explanation.definitionFit: To scrounge is to obtain something by cadging or begging, getting it however one can.

clue.text: Publications giving incitement to disorder, first to last

indicators.note: first to last means the opening letter moves to the end of the word

parts.note: sedition is speech or action inciting rebellion against authority

explanation.surface: Seditious publications urge readers to rise up against order.
explanation.walkthrough: 'first to last' moves the S of SEDITION to the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Editions are versions of a book or newspaper issued at one time, i.e. published issues.

clue.text: Market with nine, perhaps, having no dodgy deals

parts.note: a fair is a market or trade gathering
and means together with
nine is an example of a square number, three times three

explanation.surface: A honest market trader handles nine items, with no shady business.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nine, perhaps' gives SQUARE because nine is a square number (3 x 3).
explanation.definitionFit: Fair and square means honestly, without cheating or underhand dealing.

clue.text: Planning home nursing

parts.note: in means at home
tending means looking after, as in nursing the sick

explanation.surface: Someone plans to care for a patient at home.
explanation.walkthrough: IN for home comes from 'staying in'.
explanation.definitionFit: Intending means meaning or planning to do something.

clue.text: They deal crookedly and in an angry manner

indicators.note: crookedly says the letters are bent out of shape, like a cardsharp's deal

explanation.surface: Card cheats deal dishonestly and react furiously when caught.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crookedly' rearranges the eight letters of THEY DEAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Heatedly means angrily or passionately, in a fiery way.

clue.text: Make a commitment to enter the diving competition?

definitions.meaning: to commit oneself decisively to a course of action
literally, to jump into the pool as a diver does

explanation.definitionFit: Taking the plunge is an idiom for finally committing to something; literally, a plunge is a dive into water.

clue.text: Equipment around female in this room?

parts.note: kit is a set of equipment
c, short for circa, means around or approximately
a hen is a female bird

explanation.surface: A woman stands among the gadgets, where else but in this room?
explanation.walkthrough: 'around' gives C for circa, not a container. The question mark marks the definition as a hint: the room full of equipment where a woman might be found.
explanation.definitionFit: A kitchen is the room for cooking, kitted out with appliances and utensils.

clue.text: Some Californian wine given to a learner? That's a sort of mistake

parts.note: a liter, the American spelling of litre, is a measure of wine in California
L is the learner sign on British cars

explanation.surface: A novice is handed some Californian wine and makes an error.
explanation.walkthrough: LITER is the US spelling, hence 'Californian'. L is the learner plate on British cars.
explanation.definitionFit: A literal is a printing error, a misprint of a single letter.

clue.text: Form mental image of some bride at Easter

indicators.note: some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Someone pictures a bride on her Easter wedding day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'some' picks the letters running across BRIDE AT EASTER.
explanation.definitionFit: To ideate is to form an idea or picture something in the mind.

clue.text: Race by party to get money handed over?

parts.note: a do is a party or social event
a nation is a people or race

explanation.surface: A racing team pairs with a political party to secure funds.
explanation.walkthrough: DO is informal British for a party.
explanation.definitionFit: A donation is a gift of money given to a cause.

clue.text: The way deal, say, is sealed by good man?

indicators.note: is sealed by means the good man's letters close round the others on either side

parts.note: St, short for saint, is a good man
deal is pine or fir wood, so a deal tree is an example of a tree

explanation.surface: A good man confirms how an agreement was made.
explanation.walkthrough: Deal is the timber of fir or pine, so 'deal, say' points to a tree by example.
explanation.definitionFit: A street is a road, a way through a town.

clue.text: Improve, chaps, when the paper's boss comes around

indicators.note: comes around means the editor's letters enclose the word for chaps

parts.note: ED is short for editor, the newspaper's boss
men are chaps

explanation.surface: Staff improve their work when the editor visits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the paper's boss' is the editor, abbreviated in the usual crossword way.
explanation.definitionFit: To emend is to correct or improve a text.

clue.text: It probably doesn't exist — nevertheless one may be found

parts.note: yet means nevertheless or still
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A creature is probably mythical, but even so someone might come across one.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a description: a legendary creature that likely isn't real.
explanation.definitionFit: The yeti or abominable snowman is a Himalayan creature of folklore whose existence is unproven.

clue.text: Member of sect is quiet when meeting French friend

parts.note: ami is French for friend
sh is a call for quiet

explanation.surface: A sect member stays silent on meeting a French friend.
explanation.walkthrough: SH is the hushing sound that asks for quiet.
explanation.definitionFit: The Amish are a traditionalist Anabaptist Christian group, so one of them is a member of that sect.

clue.text: What's the point of an attack?

definitions.text: What's the point of an attack?

parts.words: What's the point of an attack?
parts.note: reads as a question about purpose, but literally asks for the pointed tip of a weapon used in an attack, and in another sense the leading force of an assault

explanation.definitionFit: A spearhead is the pointed tip of a spear and figuratively the leading force of an attack.

clue.text: Men heading off to drink and drug? Must be loco!

indicators.note: heading off means the first letter of men is removed

parts.note: gin is an alcoholic drink
E is slang for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: Men going off to drink and take drugs must be crazy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'loco' looks like 'crazy' but is short for locomotive. 'heading off' drops M from MEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Loco is short for locomotive, a railway engine.

clue.text: Time for outdoor fun deadly if turning out otherwise

indicators.note: turning out otherwise says the letters come out in another order

explanation.surface: An outing that could be fatal if it went another way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turning out otherwise' rearranges the eight letters of DEADLY IF.
explanation.definitionFit: A field day was originally a day of outdoor military exercises or sport, now any day of great enjoyment.
